stages.name: Provision of information
stages.title: Provision of information
stages.sub: Weigh up why governments give out information, and where this policy falls short.

steps.q: Smokers underestimate the risks and so smoke more. What could the government put on every cigarette packet to close that gap?
steps.right: Warnings and facts about the health risks
steps.wrong: A higher tax charged at the till
steps.hint: The problem here is that smokers lack knowledge, not that cigarettes are too cheap.

steps.q: Once smokers see clear health warnings on every packet, are they now better placed to weigh up the true costs before buying?
steps.right: Yes, they can now choose with full facts
steps.wrong: No, the warnings do not add anything they didn't know
steps.hint: Before the warning they were missing key facts. What changes once those facts are visible?

steps.q: Compared with building a hospital or fining every shop, how costly is printing a warning label, and is anyone forced to quit?
steps.right: Cheap, and nobody is forced to act
steps.wrong: Expensive, and everyone is forced to act
steps.hint: Think about what it costs to print a label versus running enforcement, and whether the smoker still has a free choice.

steps.q: An addicted smoker reads the warning, believes it, and still buys the next pack. Did the information change their behaviour?
steps.right: No, they carry on smoking regardless
steps.hint: Knowing the facts and being able to act on them are not always the same thing, especially with addiction.

steps.q: A vaping-risk campaign takes months to design, test and run before attitudes shift. What does that mean for cost and speed?
steps.right: It costs money and takes a long time to have an effect
steps.wrong: It is free and changes attitudes overnight
